nameStory: Watermint gets its name from its love of wet places and its distinctly minty scent. Unlike its garden cousins, this wild mint prefers to grow with its feet literally in the water, thriving along stream banks and pond edges where other mints might struggle.
description: Watermint is a sprawling perennial herb that forms dense patches in wet areas throughout New England. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall with square stems (a mint family trademark) and oval, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs. The plant produces rounded clusters of small purple or pink flowers at the stem tips and has that unmistakable fresh, cooling mint fragrance when you crush the leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded flower clusters (called heads) at the tips of stems, made up of tiny tubular purple or pink flowers that bloom from July through September

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with serrated edges, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem; crush them between your fingers for an immediate burst of fresh, cool mint scent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies in wet areas, with square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when you roll them between your fingers

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in wet locations - stream edges, pond margins, marshes, and soggy ditches where the soil stays consistently moist

habitat: Watermint thrives in consistently wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, marshes, and roadside ditches throughout New England. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other water-loving plants in areas that stay soggy year-round. It prefers partial sun to light shade and can tolerate seasonal flooding.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from spreading underground stems, with fresh green leaves appearing in late spring as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification season with full foliage and distinctive rounded flower clusters blooming from July through September, filling the air with minty fragrance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, though the mint scent remains strong in the dying foliage.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dead stems and underground rhizomes that will sprout new growth in spring.

funFact: Watermint is actually one of the parent species of peppermint - it naturally hybridized with spearmint centuries ago to create the peppermint we know today, making this wetland wanderer the wild ancestor of countless candy canes and toothpastes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other wild mints, but watermint's preference for truly wet habitats is a dead giveaway - if you find mint growing in standing water or constantly soggy soil, it's almost certainly watermint. Other mints prefer drier ground.
contextualKnowledge: Though native to Europe and Asia, watermint has naturalized in parts of North America but remains quite uncommon in New England, making any sighting noteworthy. It's sometimes called 'water spearmint' but is actually a distinct species, not a variety of true spearmint.
compareHints: Unlike Canada mint which prefers moist but not waterlogged soils, watermint truly loves having wet feet and grows right at the water's edge. Spearmint and other common mints avoid the constantly soggy conditions where watermint thrives. The rounded flower heads also distinguish it from Canada mint's more elongated flower spikes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada mint differs from its relatives by having flowers clustered in the leaf joints rather than in terminal spikes like spearmint, and it's strictly a wetland plant while corn mint tolerates drier soils.
Spearmint differs from other New England mints by its nearly hairless leaves and sweet, mild fragrance.
Unlike spearmint and peppermint which form terminal flower spikes, corn mint's flowers cluster in whorls around the stem at leaf joints.
Among New England's mints, apple mint stands out immediately for its fuzzy, rounded leaves that feel like velvet.
Horse mint differs from our common native Canada mint by being much taller and having woolly-white stems rather than smooth ones.
